extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers, ICLR authors and reviewers, peer-review/meta-researchers, conference organizers
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of ICLR 2024–2025 peer review and rebuttal dynamics, identifying what factors (textual, temporal, reviewer-level) predict score changes and which rebuttal strategies are most effective. Provides taxonomies and annotation prompts for categorizing review strengths/weaknesses and rebuttal strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review scoring dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers provide numerical scores for soundness, presentation, contribution, confidence, and an overall rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review format includes a summary, identified strengths and weaknesses, and questions for the authors alongside these numeric scores. The overall rating for ICLR 2024 and 2025 is a discrete number in {1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10} (ICLR 2026 mapped to {0,2,4,6,8,10}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall rating as primary change field
rubrics_metrics.description: Most rebuttal-induced updates occur in the overall rating field rather than detailed aspect scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 6 and discussion: 71% of cases reflect changes only in the overall score; therefore analyses of rebuttal effectiveness focus primarily on overall rating changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borderline papers sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttals primarily affect borderline papers, with score changes concentrated in the mid-range (5–6), where small shifts can change outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should prioritize rebuttals for mid-range papers because even small improvements (e.g., 5→6) can alter acceptance. The paper estimates rebuttals influence roughly one in five top papers via rank improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of rebuttal messages
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing of an author's first rebuttal message affects likelihood of score increase: middle-period submissions are most effective; very early or last-minute rebuttals have less impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 6a/6b: messages submitted in the middle of the rebuttal period (e.g., Nov 18–24) had the highest percentage (~one-third) of later score increases. Very early messages may be rushed or reflect very low initial scores; late messages have lower effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer engagement metric (conversation turns & participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer engagement — number of notes, conversation turns, and author/reviewer participation percentage — correlates with score changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews with increased scores show higher engagement and more conversation turns and stronger author–reviewer participation than keep/decrease cases. However, active discussions can also correlate with decreases, indicating variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewer influence / peer pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial scores and other reviewers' scores strongly predict rebuttal score changes; reviewers tend to converge after rebuttal (co-reviewer influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer convergence decreases disagreement by roughly 9–10% overall, and much more for high-quality categories (oral/spotlight). The paper formalizes co-reviewer influence as pairwise disagreement |si−sj| and reports normalized after−before differences divided by score range (9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer ordering effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The order (timestamp) of review submission correlates with score generosity: the reviewer who submits last (displayed first) tends to give higher scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 4a/4c: across 4-review papers, distributions show increasing generosity in reviewers ordered by submission time (Reviewer 4→1). This is an observed bias practitioners should be aware of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer disagreement / normalization metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer disagreement per paper computed as average pairwise |si−sj| across reviewer pairs; normalized difference (after−before)/9 indicates strength of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger decreases (negative ∆) indicate stronger co-reviewer influence. Table 3 reports absolute and relative changes by submission category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement in ranking as acceptance proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how rebuttal score changes displace papers in top-% ranking (proxy for acceptance) to gauge impact on final outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2: over 40% of papers in the top 5% before rebuttal are replaced after score updates. Rebuttals have greater effect when acceptance rates are low (more displacement). Ranking is used as a proxy and meta-review factors are noted as additional influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection requirement to measure score changes
rubrics_metrics.description: To track rebuttal-induced score changes on OpenReview, archive review data both immediately after initial reviews and again after the rebuttal period because OpenReview displays only final versions (preliminary reviews are overwritten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corpus construction requires collecting before- and after-rebuttal scores at release times; failure to archive initial reviews will lose preliminary scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual taxonomy for weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured taxonomy for labeling review weaknesses with main categories and subcategories (Novelty & Contribution; Motivation; Methodology & Technical Soundness; Experiments & Evaluation; Results; Data; Writing & Presentation; Broader Impact, Ethics & Relevance; References & Related Work; Fit & Scope; Other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators must map every weakness paragraph to a main category and a subcategory (use 'Other' only when impossible), extract the exact span, and annotate multiple weaknesses per paragraph. Appendix/Figure 11 provides full subcategories and the annotation prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual taxonomy for strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: A parallel structured taxonomy for labeling review strengths (same top-level categories as weaknesses but with positive subcategories: e.g., Original idea/high novelty; Strong baselines; Thorough ablations; Clear presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators follow similar rules to weaknesses: map to a main category and subcategory, extract span, and annotate every strength paragraph. Appendix/Figure 12 provides details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer–Author stance & strategy annotation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-field annotation scheme for reviewer-author interactions: coverage (Answered/Not Answered), stance (Agree/Disagree with defined subcategories), and strategy (evidence_backed_clarification vs generic_defense_vague with subcategories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each reviewer weakness/question, annotate coverage, stance subcategory (e.g., evasion, reject_validity, completion_claim, future_work, etc.), and strategy subcategory (method_details, new_table_figures, analysis, experiments_in_paper, new_experiments, citation, repetition, broad_assertion, future_promise, bare_agreement_or_disagreement). See Appendix/Figure 13 prompt for exact definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-backed clarification vs generic/vague defense (rebuttal strategy distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify rebuttal content as either evidence-backed clarification (provides method details, new experiments, analysis, new figures/tables, citations) or generic/vague defense (repetition, broad assertions, evasion, vague future promises, bare agreement/disagreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence-backed clarifications are associated with positive score changes; generic/vague defenses and evasive stances tend to result in 'keep' or no improvement. Table 8 and discussion show these strategies' predictive coefficients for INC/KEEP/DEC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy subcategories that improve scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific rebuttal actions associated with score increases: evidence-backed clarifications such as method_details, new_experiments, new_table_figures, analysis, and concrete citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multinomial logistic regression and feature importance (Table 8) indicate these strategy features have positive coefficients for increasing scores. 'Bare agreement/disagreement' can also help relative to vague defenses, but is weaker than evidence-backed actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy subcategories that hinder score change
rubrics_metrics.description: Evasive stances and generic/vague defenses (broad assertions, repetition, future promises without specifics, bare agreement without evidence) are associated with keeping or not improving scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 8 shows generic/vague defense and evasion features have coefficients correlated with KEEP or DEC classes; the discussion warns authors against 'evasive stance' and 'generic/vague defense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive features for score-change models
rubrics_metrics.description: Top predictive features for whether a review's score will increase include: initial overall rating, mean overall rating of other reviewers, reviewer engagement (number of notes), contribution and soundness scores, reviewer confidence, and textual/strategy features (evidence-backed clarification, generic/vague defense, method details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretability-focused models (multinomial logistic regression) are recommended to identify feature importance. Table 8 and Table 4 list top features and their average absolute coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count signals in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Word counts of review sections are correlated with scores: longer strengths sections correlate positively with higher overall ratings; longer weaknesses sections correlate negatively; reviewers with higher confidence write longer weaknesses and give lower overall ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 8 and Table 5 show correlation heatmaps and average word counts by submission category. Word count is a strong feature for classifying score groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common specific weakness examples to address
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent criticisms in low-rated papers include: writing flaws (unclear wording, poor structure), insufficient/weak baselines, too few datasets/limited domain, unclear algorithmic description, missing ablations, weak theoretical justification, unrealistic assumptions, reproducibility issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 9 enumerates top subcategories per rating group; authors should prioritize addressing these concrete issues in rebuttals with evidence-backed clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common specific strength examples to highlight
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent praises in high-rated papers include: originality/high novelty, significant contribution, clear and meaningful improvement over prior work, strong methodology/theoretical justification, elegant and efficient models, realistic/large-scale experiments, thorough ablations, clear presentation and strong figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 10 enumerates strengths per rating group; authors should emphasize these aspects in the paper and in rebuttals when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal coverage requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When annotating or assessing rebuttals, determine whether each reviewer concern was addressed (coverage) and mark Not Answered when no response exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Not Answered, leave stance/strategy empty; otherwise, annotate stance and strategy. This is both an annotation rule and a practical guideline: unanswered concerns are unlikely to change scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal dynamics of reviewer activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer writing activity is highly concentrated near reviewer deadlines; reviewer/author activity peaks during specific rebuttal period days and is shaped by deadlines and committee prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 5 and 6 show daily activity patterns. Authors and organizers should be aware that reviewer responses and engagement often cluster near deadlines and shortly after review release (many changes occur within first hour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and interpreting score-displacement effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify percentage of papers displaced from top-% thresholds after rebuttal-induced score changes to measure potential acceptance impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displacement curves (Figure 2) across thresholds to estimate how rebuttals affect rankings; note that ranking is a proxy and other factors (meta-reviewer judgment, topic fit) also determine acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation instruction constraint: avoid 'Other' unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators must not use the 'Other' category for strengths/weaknesses unless absolutely impossible to map to a defined category or subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a weak or partial connection (~1%) should map to an existing category. This is part of the annotation prompt constraints (Figures 11–12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability preference for modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interpretable models (e.g., multinomial logistic regression) to study which review/rebuttal features influence scores because they allow inspecting coefficients/feature importances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors selected multinomial logistic regression for interpretability; macro-F1 and feature importances are reported to justify conclusions about influential features.
